title: The text of the poem
short: The first two stanzas are a separate lyric in Blake's Notebook; the engraved Songs of Experience poem begins 'I went to the Garden of Love'.
body: In Blake's illuminated Songs of Experience (1794), 'The Garden of Love' has three stanzas only, beginning at l. 9 here. The eight lines beginning 'I laid me down upon a bank' are a separate poem in Blake's Notebook (the Rossetti Manuscript); modern editors such as Erdman print it separately among the Notebook poems. Some older printed texts, like the one in the archive, joined the two. The Notebook lines are thematically close: Love asleep, weeping, and the waste places of the fallen world. Students should cite the engraved three-stanza text as the published poem.

title: Love asleep; rushes dank
short: Love lies asleep, and among damp rushes there is weeping: a pastoral scene of passion repressed or neglected.
body: 'Dank' means unpleasantly damp. The sleeping figure of Love may be Cupid or Eros, a familiar pastoral motif, but Blake's sleep is ominous, a suspension of vital energy. The weeping in the rushes is not explained, which is typical of Blake's lyrics: it may be the voices of the 'beguiled' in the next stanza. Read with the engraved poem, the lines suggest a world in which love has been put to sleep by prohibition.

title: thistles and thorns
short: The curse on the ground after the Fall: 'Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee' (Genesis 3:18).
body: The 'heath', 'wild' and 'waste' are uncultivated land, the fallen world outside Eden. In Genesis 3:18 God curses the ground after Adam's sin. Blake's figures are 'driven out', like Adam and Eve expelled from the garden (Genesis 3:24). The heath could also suggest the commons being enclosed in Blake's time, though this reading is a critical suggestion rather than a certainty.

title: beguiled ... compelled to the chaste
short: Eve says 'The serpent beguiled me' (Genesis 3:13); here the beguilers have deceived lovers into a forced chastity.
body: Blake reverses the biblical story: the deception is not temptation to sin but persuasion into self-denial. 'Compelled to the chaste' uses the adjective as a noun, 'compelled to join the chaste' or 'to chastity'. Blake's hostility to enforced chastity is a constant theme, as in the Proverbs of Hell in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell ('Prisons are built with stones of Law, Brothels with bricks of Religion') and in Visions of the Daughters of Albion (1793).

anchor: went to the Garden of Love
title: The Garden of Love
short: The garden recalls Eden and the enclosed garden of the Song of Songs; here the engraved Experience poem begins.
body: The Song of Solomon 4:12 calls the beloved 'A garden inclosed', and medieval allegory made the garden of love a place of courtship (as in the Roman de la Rose). For Blake the garden is also Eden, and the speaker's childhood green, the free play of Innocence. 'Saw what I never had seen' marks the speaker's arrival at Experience. Critics have read the poem as an attack on the Church of England's sexual morality and on institutional religion generally; others stress personal repression, the internalised law.

title: in the midst
short: The chapel stands where the tree of life and the tree of knowledge stood 'in the midst of the garden' (Genesis 2:9; 3:3).
body: In Genesis 2:9 the tree of life and the tree of knowledge of good and evil are 'in the midst of the garden', and 3:3 repeats the prohibition of that tree. Blake replaces the tree with a chapel, so that religion itself becomes the place of prohibition. A 'chapel' may suggest a Dissenting chapel or a chapel of ease of the established Church; critics differ on whether Blake has a specific denomination in mind or means organised religion generally.

title: the green
short: The village green of childhood play recalls 'The Ecchoing Green' of Songs of Innocence.
body: In Songs of Innocence 'The Ecchoing Green' celebrates children playing on a common green watched by the old. The Experience poem builds a chapel on that space. The contrast of the two volumes, 'shewing the two contrary states of the human soul' (as Blake's title page puts it), is enacted within a single line. The plate design shows mourners kneeling at a tomb, which supports the reading of play turned into mourning.

title: Thou shalt not
short: The formula of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20) written over the chapel door: religion as negative law.
body: Eight of the Ten Commandments in Exodus 20:3-17 begin 'Thou shalt not'. Blake consistently opposed what he saw as a religion of prohibition to the gospel of forgiveness and energy; in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell he has Jesus break the commandments, acting 'from impulse, not from rules'. The shut gates contrast with the open, playing green. Some critics hear in the shut gates a reference to the custom of keeping churches locked except at services.

title: flowers and tombstones
short: The garden that bore flowers is now full of graves; 'tombstones where flowers should be'.
body: Flowers in Blake often stand for natural desires and their fulfilment (compare 'Ah! Sun-flower' and 'My Pretty Rose Tree' in the same volume). The substitution of tombstones means that desire, denied, has died. The garden becomes a churchyard, the burial ground beside a church, so that the space of love becomes the space of death. The end-rhyme that 'be' leads us to expect is never supplied; the last two lines rhyme inwardly instead (gowns/rounds, briars/desires), a formal sign of the frustration the image describes.

sources.cite: Andrew Lincoln, ed., Songs of Innocence and of Experience (William Blake Trust / Tate Gallery, 1991), commentary

title: graves
short: The garden is a graveyard: repression kills joys as death kills bodies.
body: Critics read the graves as the buried desires of those 'compelled to the chaste', and also as the literal deaths that religion, in Blake's view, makes its central concern (the priest's office for burial). The plate's design of kneeling mourners at a tomb makes the connection visual. The line's simple syntax ('And I saw') keeps the visionary tone of the narrative.

title: priests in black gowns
short: Clergy in black gowns patrolling like watchmen: 'walking their rounds' suggests a beat or a jailer's inspection.
body: The black gown was the dress of Anglican clergy when preaching, and also of Dissenting ministers, so the image covers clergy generally. 'Rounds' are the regular patrols of a watchman or warder, implying surveillance. Blake's anticlericalism appears throughout the Songs of Experience, for example in 'The Little Vagabond' and 'London'. Erdman reads the poem within the radical politics of the 1790s; Glen stresses the critique of a morality internalised as well as imposed.

title: The lengthened last lines
short: The last two lines lengthen and add internal rhymes (gowns/rounds, briars/desires), so the verse itself seems bound and constrained.
body: The poem's anapaestic lines are fairly regular until the final couplet, which grows longer and carries internal rhymes in place of the expected end-rhymes with 'be'. Critics have heard in the dragging, rhyming line the effect of binding: the sound mimics the action. Briars (thorny shrubs) recall the curse on the earth (Genesis 3:18) and perhaps the crown of thorns. 'Joys and desires' ends the poem with what has been bound, not with those who bind.
